ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. text:
Corn in Cambodia only occasionally shows clear micronutrient deficiency, but zinc (Zn), boron (B), and molybdenum (Mo) are the ones most likely to limit growth when they do occur. Zinc deficiency shows up as pale striping (interveinal chlorosis) on young leaves near the base of the plant and shortened internodes ("little leaf" appearance); it is more likely on soils with high pH or where phosphorus fertilizer has been used heavily, since high P can reduce zinc uptake. Where zinc deficiency is confirmed (by soil test or visible symptoms), it can be corrected with a zinc sulfate soil or foliar application.

Because most Cambodian soils sampled under this project were also found to test low in phosphorus and molybdenum, and to often need supplemental potassium and magnesium, a soil test is the most reliable way to know whether a particular field needs micronutrient correction, rather than relying on visual symptoms alone, which can be easy to confuse with other stresses.
